title: India Is Hosting Iran, Russia, and China Under One Roof While American Missiles Hit the Gulf. Welcome to the BRICS Presidency.
excerpt: As ministerial meetings stack up across Delhi and Nagpur ahead of September's summit, India's BRICS chairmanship is becoming a real-time test of Modi's diplomatic balancing act — with the diaspora's safety and prosperity on the line.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's BRICS chairmanship is a diplomatic balancing act amid US-Iran tensions.
  • The September summit will showcase India's leadership among 11 BRICS nations.
  • India aims to position itself as the voice of the Global South.
  • Nine million Indians in the Gulf face risks from escalating regional conflicts.
  • India's diplomatic efforts are crucial for the safety and prosperity of its diaspora.

India is in the middle of the most consequential diplomatic sprint of Modi's third term, and it is happening under the BRICS flag. Over the past week, New Delhi has hosted a rapid-fire series of ministerial meetings — transport, national security, academia, foreign affairs — as it builds toward the 18th BRICS Summit in September, the biggest multilateral gathering India has chaired since the G20 in 2023. The scheduling alone is a statement of ambition. On Saturday, Union Minister Nitin Gadkari opened a two-day BRICS Transport Ministers' meeting in Nagpur, bringing together delegates from all eleven member states — Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates — to negotiate frameworks for sustainable transport, clean mobility, and logistics resilience. Separately, Prime Minister Narendra Modi held bilateral meetings with the foreign ministers of Russia, Iran, and Brazil, stacking diplomatic bandwidth in a way that telegraphs India's intent to be more than a ceremonial chair. ## The Iran Factor > **"US Ambassador Sergio Gor confirmed the visit and said the trade pact would be wrapped up "sooner rather than later." A Trump state visit to India is projected for 2027."** The elephant in the room — or rather, the war in the strait — is Iran. As India hosts ministerial meetings where Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi is expected to participate, American and Iranian forces are exchanging missile strikes across the Persian Gulf. Iran has re-closed the Strait of Hormuz, one Indian crew member is missing after an attack on a container ship off Oman, and nine million Indians across the Gulf states are living under the shadow of an expanding conflict. India's diplomatic tightrope is not new, but BRICS makes it sharper. Iran is now a full BRICS member, seated at the same table as India. The United States, India's closest defence partner, is at war with Iran. India imports 85 percent of its crude oil and has historically relied on both Iranian supply and American goodwill. Hosting Iran's senior diplomats in Delhi while American airstrikes hit Bandar Abbas is a balancing act that few countries could attempt — and that only India's BRICS chairmanship requires. India's National Security Adviser Ajit Doval held talks with Iran's Deputy Secretary for Defence Affairs, Ghadir Nezamipour, on the sidelines of the 16th BRICS NSAs' Meeting in Delhi. The subtext was unmistakable: India wants to keep a diplomatic channel to Tehran open, even as it condemns attacks on commercial shipping and demands the safe return of its missing sailor. ## What the September Summit Means The summit, scheduled for September 12–13 under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," will be India's moment to prove that the expanded BRICS bloc — now eleven nations representing 45 percent of the world's population and roughly 37 percent of global GDP — can function as more than a talking shop. India has a specific agenda: positioning itself as the voice of the Global South. The academic mid-term conference highlighted India's "humanity-first" vision, a phrase that Modi has used to differentiate India's BRICS chairmanship from China's more transactional 2024 presidency and Brazil's ideologically charged 2025 turn. Whether this rhetoric translates into deliverables — a BRICS grain reserve, a digital payments corridor, a shared logistics framework — will be tested in September.
Diplomatic Challenges Ahead
›Iran is a full BRICS member amid US-Iran tensions.
›India imports 85% of its crude oil.
›Modi's agenda includes a BRICS grain reserve and digital payments.
›US trade agreement expected to finalize by December.
The diplomatic calendar does not stop there. Modi is also expected to visit the United States in December for the G20 summit in Miami, where the India-US trade agreement is expected to be near completion. US Ambassador Sergio Gor confirmed the visit and said the trade pact would be wrapped up "sooner rather than later." A Trump state visit to India is projected for 2027. ## What It Means for the Diaspora For the five million Indians in the US and millions more across the Gulf, UK, Canada, and Australasia, the BRICS build-up matters in ways that rarely make the front page. India's ability to maintain working relationships with both Washington and Tehran determines whether Indian workers in the Gulf are evacuated safely, whether Indian energy prices stay manageable, and whether the remittance corridors that fund families back home remain open. The BRICS transport ministers' discussions in Nagpur, for instance, touch directly on freight and logistics corridors that Indian exporters and small businesses depend on. The digital payments conversations could eventually allow Indian workers in BRICS countries to send money home at lower cost. And India's insistence on a "rules-based" approach to the Strait of Hormuz — echoed at the IMO Council last week, which condemned Iran's sovereignty claim over the waterway — is ultimately about protecting the livelihoods of the 200,000 Indian seafarers who transit those waters. Modi's BRICS presidency is not a photo opportunity. It is a live-fire diplomatic exercise, conducted against the backdrop of a Gulf war, a global inflation spike, and a US midterm election. The September summit will be the test. The ministerial meetings this week are the dress rehearsal.
